\section{Introduction to the Operational View}

The Operational View describes how the Human Benchmark system will be operated,
administered, and supported when running in its production environment. This
view is critical for ensuring that the system functions reliably in day-to-day
operation, addressing aspects such as maintenance, monitoring, and
support.

The Operational Viewpoint focuses on concerns related to the ongoing operation
of the system after deployment. It bridges the gap between system
development and production usage, ensuring that the system can be effectively
managed throughout its lifecycle.

The primary stakeholders for the Operational View include:
\begin{table}[H]
    \centering
    \caption{Primary Stakeholders for the Operational View}
    \label{tab:operational_view_stakeholders}
    \begin{tabular}{|p{0.3\textwidth}|p{0.6\textwidth}|}
        \hline
        \textbf{Stakeholder}  & \textbf{Role in the Operational View}                        \\ \hline
        System Administrators & Responsible for installation, configuration, and maintenance \\ \hline
        Production Engineers  & Handle deployment and operational monitoring                 \\ \hline
        Support Staff         & Provide assistance to users                                  \\ \hline
        Developers            & Need to understand operational considerations                \\ \hline
        Testers               & Verify operational aspects                                   \\ \hline
        Assessors             & Evaluate operational capabilities and risks                  \\ \hline
    \end{tabular}
\end{table}

This view is particularly important for the Human Benchmark system, as it
requires reliable operation to support both single-player and multiplayer
experiences with real-time interaction.

\section{Core Architectural Elements of the Operational View}

\subsection{Installation and Upgrade Process}

The Human Benchmark system employs a containerized deployment approach to
installation and upgrade. This strategy
provides consistency across environments and simplifies the deployment process.

\subsubsection{Installation Components}

The system installation is organized into the following component groups:

\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Frontend Components}: React-based user interface components deployed as container images
    \item \textbf{Backend API Components}: ASP.NET Core services packaged as container images
    \item \textbf{Database Components}: PostgreSQL database schema definitions and migration scripts
    \item \textbf{WebSocket Services}: Real-time communication components for multiplayer features
    \item \textbf{Configuration Files}: Environment-specific configuration for services
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Installation Strategy}

The installation process is managed through a CI/CD pipeline that follows these steps:

\begin{figure}[H]
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=0.8\textwidth]{AutomationAndSections/Sections/7operationalView/Images/Deployment Diagram.drawio.png}
    \caption{Deployment Diagram: Human Benchmark Installation and Upgrade Process Flow}
    \label{fig:deployment_diagram}
\end{figure}

Below is a more detailed version of versioning sequence diagram:

\begin{figure}[H]
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=0.8\textwidth]{AutomationAndSections/Sections/7operationalView/Images/Versioning.drawio.png}
    \caption{Versioning Sequence Diagram: Detailed Flow of Version Management in Human Benchmark System}
    \label{fig:versioning_sequence_diagram}
\end{figure}

From this diagram, we can see that we have 5 stages:

The five stages of the process are as follows:

\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Build Application}: The application is built from the source
          code. During this stage, developers have the option to include a specific
          message in their commit to trigger the versioning process, ensuring that the
          build is appropriately tagged and tracked.

    \item \textbf{Test (Integration and Unit)}: Comprehensive testing is
          conducted, including both integration and unit tests, to validate the
          functionality and reliability of the application. This ensures that the
          application meets quality standards before proceeding to the next stages.

    \item \textbf{Dockerize}: The application is packaged into Docker
          containers. This step ensures consistency across environments and simplifies
          deployment by encapsulating all dependencies and configurations within the
          container.

    \item \textbf{Update Database}: Database updates are manually triggered
          using a special commit message. This ensures that schema changes or
          migrations are applied in a controlled manner, minimizing the risk of errors
          during deployment.

    \item \textbf{Deploy Application to MIF OpenNebula}: The final stage
          involves deploying the application to the MIF OpenNebula environment. This
          step ensures that the application is made available in the production
          environment, ready for end-user access.
\end{enumerate}

\subsubsection{Upgrade Process}

The upgrade process is exactly the same as the installation process.
The only difference is that the developer must ensure that the database migration
is applied correctly otherwise the CI/CD pipeline will fail.

\subsubsection{Rollback Strategy}

In case CI/CD pipeline fails during the upgrade process, simpply nothing will be
deployed to the production environment. A red symbol will appear near the commit
to indicate that the CI/CD failed. If CI/CD succeeds but later on issues are
detected, the rollback must be performed manually by the system administrator.

\subsection{Operational Monitoring and Control}

Currently we have no monitoring in place, but we plan to use Graphana and
Elasticsearch combined with Prometheus for monitoring and alerting.

\subsubsection{Monitoring Approach}

We have defined a monitoring approach that includes:

\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Infrastructure Monitoring}: Docker commands to check container status
    \item \textbf{Application Performance Monitoring}: Response times, error rates, and throughput metrics
    \item \textbf{Database Monitoring}: Query performance, connection pools, and storage utilization using Aiven Console
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Control Capabilities}

System administrators have access to the following control capabilities:

\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Service Management}: Start, stop, and restart individual services using MIF OpenNebula
    \item \textbf{Scaling Controls}: Adjust resource allocation for components under load using MIF OpenNebula
    \item \textbf{Configuration Updates}: Apply configuration changes without redeployment using SSH to the server
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Alerting System}

\subsubsection{Alert Categories}

The Human Benchmark alerting system classifies alerts into the following categories:

\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Technical Alerts}: Infrastructure, application, or database issues
    \item \textbf{Performance Alerts}: Degradation in system performance metrics
    \item \textbf{Capacity Alerts}: Resource utilization approaching defined thresholds
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Alert Routing and Prioritization}
Currently we do not have the capibility to route and prioritize alerts using
email or sms, so we will simply display them in the Graphana or Elasticsearch
dashboard.

\subsubsection{Alert Management}

To prevent alert fatigue, the system implements:

\begin{itemize}
    \item Automatic suppression of duplicate alerts
    \item Configurable thresholds based on time of day and user load
    \item Alert history for tracking recurring issues
\end{itemize}

    \item \textbf{Database Performance}: Query execution time and connection utilization
          % \item \textbf{WebSocket Performance}: Connection reliability and message delivery time

\end{itemize}

\subsection{Configuration Management}

\subsubsection{Configuration Groups}

The Human Benchmark system organizes configuration into the following groups:

\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Application Configuration}: Core application settings across services (port numbers)
    \item \textbf{Database Configuration}: PostgreSQL settings and connection parameters (names, passwords)
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Configuration Value Sets}
We have no plans for this as our user base is +20 users and we do not expect
any significant load on the system.

In case any configuration changes happen, we will first test the application
with these changes locally, then we will push these changes to the production
branch of the repository. After that, we will run the CI/CD pipeline to deploy the configuration changes.
We think that this is sufficient for our simple application.

\subsection{Support Model}

% \subsubsection{Support Tiers}
We do not have any support tiers, as we are a small team and we do not have the
resources to provide tiered support. We can only provide basic support through
email and Discord channels. We may use screenshots or screen sharing using
Discord to help users with their issues. We may also use GitLab wiki to provide documentation and guides for users.

Additionally, we will use GitLab issues to track bugs, feature requests, and
incidents. This will allow us to classify and prioritize incidents based on
their impact, assign them to the appropriate team members, and track their
resolution. For more complex issues, we may use screenshots or screen sharing
via Discord to assist users. Analytics from GitLab issues will help us identify
recurring problems and improve our processes over time.

Furthermore, we will use GitLab To-do and Milestone features to manage task
assignments, track progress, and ensure timely resolution of issues and feature
implementations.

\subsection{Backup and Restore}

\subsubsection{Backup Strategy}

We use a very simple backup strategy that is sufficient for our current needs.

\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Database Backups}:
          \begin{itemize}
              \item Full database backups daily
          \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Configuration Backups}:
          \begin{itemize}
              \item System configuration backed up after each change
          \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Repository Backups}:
          \begin{itemize}
              \item GitLab repository backed up to GitHub for redundancy
          \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Backup Storage}

Backups are stored with the following considerations:

\begin{itemize}
    \item Database backups in the same cloud.
    \item Configuration backups locally on development machines.
    \item Repository backups in GitHub storage for redundancy.
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Restore Capabilities}

The system supports several restore scenarios:

\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Database Recovery}: Using Aiven Console to restore PostgreSQL backups
    \item \textbf{Full System Recovery}: Triggering a full CI/CD pipeline run to redeploy the system
    \item \textbf{Configuration Recovery}: Simply copying configuration files from local backups
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Data Consistency}
Right now, we only back up the database to keep our data safe. While this helps
protect important information, it doesn't cover possible mismatches between the
database and other parts of the system, like configuration files, application
state, or cached data. For example, if the code is updated but the database is
not, the system might not work correctly. To fix this, we need a better backup
and restore plan that includes all key parts of the system. This will make sure
everything stays in sync and can be fully restored without issues.

\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Cloud Provider Integration}

The system integrates with cloud provider services:

\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Monitoring Integration}: MIF OpenNebula and Aiven provide built-in monitoring capabilities
    \item \textbf{Scaling}: MIF OpenNebula provides scaling capabilities for VM
\end{itemize}

\section{Impact of Key Perspectives on the Operational View}

\subsection{Impact of Availability and Resilience Perspective}

Applying the Availability and Resilience perspective to the Operational View of
the Human Benchmark system has several significant impacts:

\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Enhanced Monitoring}: The monitoring system has been expanded
    to include detailed health checks for all components. This ensures that any
    potential issues affecting system availability are detected quickly.

    \item \textbf{Robust Backup Strategy}: The backup and restore capabilities
    have been designed with multiple storage locations to minimize data loss in
    failure scenarios. 

    \item \textbf{Cloud Deployment Architecture}: The system is designed to run
    on MIF OpenNebula and Aiven, which provides built-in redundancy capabilities
    (backups). This ensures that the system can recover quickly from
    infrastructure failures. It also supports scaling to handle increased user
    load without impacting performance.

    \item \textbf{Installation and Upgrade Process}: The installation and
    upgrade processes use GitLab CI/CD pipelines to automate deployments and 
    ensure quick delivery of updates.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Impact of Performance and Scalability Perspective}

The Performance and Scalability perspective has significantly shaped the Operational View in the following ways:

\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Comprehensive Performance Monitoring}: The monitoring system
    has been designed to track system performance metrics such as CPU, memory,
    and network usage, as well as error rates and response times. This allows
    for quick identification of performance bottlenecks and errors.

    \item \textbf{Configuration Management}: We can quickly adjust configuration and trigger
    CI/CD pipelines to deploy changes without downtime.

    \item \textbf{Auto-scaling Design}: MIF OpenNebula and Aiven provide
    scalling capabilities that allow the system to adjust to changing user loads.

    % \item \textbf{Database Performance Optimization}: The operational procedures include specific monitoring and maintenance routines for database optimization, such as index maintenance and query performance analysis, to ensure that leaderboard and historical data queries remain efficient as the dataset grows.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Impact of Security Perspective}

key impacts:

\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Alerting System}: The alerting system has been designed to
    detect errors and anomalies that may indicate security incidents. these
    alerts are displayed in the Graphana or Elasticsearch dashboard.

    % include immutable storage and encryption to protect against ransomware and
    % data theft, ensuring that backups cannot be compromised even if the primary
    % system is breached.

    \item \textbf{Secure Configuration Management}: The configurations are stored
    locally on development machines and are version-controlled in GitLab. As a result
    of this, we can ensure that configuration changes are tracked and can be
    audited. This helps prevent unauthorized changes that could compromise system
    security.

    \item \textbf{Operational Monitoring}: The monitoring to monitor system
    utilization and performance. This allows us to detect potential DDoS attacks
    or other security threats that could impact system availability or
    performance.
\end{itemize}

\section{Importance and Justification of the Operational View for Human Benchmark}

The Operational View ensures the Human Benchmark system runs smoothly and
reliably in its daily use. It focuses on key aspects like installation,
monitoring, backups, and performance to meet the needs of administrators,
software engineers, and users. This view is essential for maintaining system
availability, handling updates, and ensuring accurate performance measurements.
Without it, the system could face downtime, data loss, or performance issues,
impacting user trust and satisfaction.
